rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 and 3 report own greenhouse inoculation experiments (repeated twice), spectroradiometer measurements, index development, a field experiment at Klein-Altendorf and hyperspectral imaging. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 3 report that the developed SDIs had higher classification accuracy than common vegetation indices, e.g. HI 89.0% vs NDVI 80.3% for healthy vs diseased, CLSI 92.4% vs NDVI 73.4% for Cercospora; SVIs were unsuitable (50%) for rust and powdery mildew; Section 3.4 and Fig. 5 report HI applied to canopy-scale field data with 81.63% accuracy. Q7: Section 3.4 and Discussion state that, because of differing light conditions and sensors, the threshold value must be optimised individually for each dataset before classification; Section 2.4 states the normalised wavelength difference is mandatory for a specific index. Q8: Section 3.4 states that disease-specific classification was not suitable in the field because of mixed infections; Results, Discussion and Conclusion state difficulties remained at early infection stages/low severities (classification errors of 51-97% at 1-2% severity, Table 2), and that applicability to datasets under changing conditions involves several difficulties.
rows.notes: The passage is about detection and differentiation accuracy, which the study tests directly; the pest_control function is treated as encompassing disease detection. Caveat: the SDI-versus-NDVI comparison was made only on controlled leaf-scale greenhouse data; under field conditions only the generic health-index was applied (81.63%), no comparison with NDVI was made there, and disease-specific differentiation was not feasible in the field, so the 'real world field conditions' qualifier is only partly supported. Q3: the same spectral-index classification approach was applied with different sensors (leaf spectroradiometer, imaging spectrograph, canopy spectroradiometer), which is one method; visual severity scoring was used only as ground truth. Q4: disease-specific reflectance changes were measured (Fig. 2) but the physiological mechanism (pigment, structure changes) is cited rather than measured. Q5: one crop, one cultivar, one greenhouse setting plus one field site. Q6: the field experiment is a single field at one research station. Q9: accuracies, precisions and recalls are given without standard deviations or confidence intervals; standard deviations in Fig. 2 refer to reflectance, not to the accuracy result.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2 and 3 report the authors' own greenhouse experiments, field measurements and hyperspectral imaging data.
rows.notes: The study shows that spectral disease indices classify healthy and diseased sugar beet leaves more accurately than common vegetation indices (Table 3) and can be applied to field and imaging data; it reports nothing on yield, fruit quality or crop production, nor on management actions taken on the basis of detection. Disease detection is only a precondition of the claimed crop production effect.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Supplementary appendices A-C are referenced but not included.
